say: Welcome to puzzle day! There are four puzzle cards: coins, patterns, logic and measuring. With every card we use the four inquirer rules: notice, test, check, explain.
Whiteboard round: I ask a quick question from one of our lessons. Everybody writes the answer at the same time and keeps the board low. Nobody is put on the spot. “I am not sure” is fine.
Look at the four puzzle cards. Which do you think will be hardest? Write your guess. Each pair chooses ONE card for 6 minutes, then you swap. Reporting back is optional.
stuck: Stuck: say the inquirer rule that might help.
Rushing: “Check your answer a different way before you move on.”
For pairs who want more: make a puzzle for the other pair, then swap.

say: “Coins: make 45¢ using exactly 3 coins from 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ and 50¢. I try 20 + 20 + 5 = 45. ✓ Three coins.”
“Pattern: 5, 8, 11, 14 … The rule is add 3. I make a table of places 1 to 10 and keep adding 3: 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26, 29, 32. The 10th number is 32.”

do: Ask: “Which inquirer rule helps you here?”
Ask: “How do you know your answer is right? Show me.”
Ask: “What would you do differently next time?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Which lesson does this remind you of?”
Hint 3: “Explain it to your partner out loud.”

say: “Swap the puzzle you wrote (workbook Q9) with a partner and solve it.”
“Which puzzle was hardest? What helped you when you were stuck?”
ask: “Swap the puzzle you wrote (workbook Q9) with a partner and solve it.”
Open answers. Listen for the inquirer rules: noticing a pattern, testing with objects, checking and explaining.

say: “You are real inquirers now. Here are your certificates.”
Say it once to the group, then give each child a certificate and one specific thing they did well (about 10 seconds each).

l10-title.note: Objective: Use patterns, bonds, graphs, money, shapes, logic, working backwards and measuring in new puzzles, and explain the thinking. Materials: The four puzzle cards (coins, patterns, logic, measuring), play coins, cubes, mini whiteboards, certificates, stamps. Online: each pair chooses a card from the workbook page. Reporting back is optional: say one thing you tried, not the answer. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up game and whiteboard round 2 to 6 (five questions), sneak-peek puzzles 6 to 10, explore 10 to 28, teaching 28 to 37 (how to start a puzzle: draw it, list it, make a table; click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 37 to 41, worksheet 41 to 71 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it (a 30-second stand-and-stretch reset after the page-1 check, taken from that slot; the last 4 minutes check page 2, after a 1-minute stand-up stretch), talk time 71 to 79, exit ticket 79 to 87, look-back 87 to 90 (this lesson has no spare minutes: follow the shortened plan, see the guide). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose, any time or at home. Nobody is told which page they should be on.

l10-warm1.note: Minutes 2 to 6. Whiteboard round. Say: "Everybody writes the answer at the same time. There is no passing round and nobody is put on the spot. If you are not sure, write a guess or draw it." Ask one question at a time, give thinking time, then click to show the answer to everyone. If answers differ, say "Different ideas are a good thing to talk about." Never groan at a wrong answer. Answers: 20; 6; 10¢ + 5¢ (or 5¢ + 5¢ + 5¢ is three coins); triangle; 7.

l10-warmcheck.note: Minutes 6 to 10 (4 minutes). SAY (about 26 words, once): "Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked." Question 1 is an access question: every child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone starts with a win. Question 2 makes you think. Children try both on their own paper (about a minute each). Then everyone answers ONCE, after the second question: face to face, each child keeps the paper low so only the tutor sees it; online, children say the answers together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). There are no private chat messages. Never use boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera, and never read out or compare anyone's answer. Do not write scores down or announce them. Then click to show each answer to the whole group and say "Lots of us had a different idea, and that is fine." Look for good ideas to praise in a later lesson; do not keep a list of who found question 2 easy. When the worksheet starts (minute 41) invite the WHOLE group (“When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation”), never one child by name. Everyone joins Explore and the Mini-lesson. Answers: 1) 24 and 29. The rule is add 5. 2) 20¢ + 10¢ + 5¢. (It is the only way.)

l10-explore1.note: Minutes 10 to 11. Explain the plan, then move to the next slide with the four puzzle cards. Each pair works on ONE card for 6 minutes (11 to 17), you give 1 minute to swap (17 to 18), then a 4-minute second round (18 to 22), then ONE debrief question and 20-second pair reports (22 to 28). Pairs read their own card: do not read all four aloud. A pair that is still stuck keeps its card for round 2. Materials: the four puzzle cards (workbook Puzzle cards page), play coins, cubes, mini whiteboards. Online: each pair chooses a card from the workbook page. Reporting back is optional: say one thing you tried, not the answer.

l10-cards.note: Minutes 11 to 17. Each pair works on ONE puzzle card for 6 minutes (the printed cards are on the Puzzle cards page of the workbook; online, each pair chooses a card). Pairs read their own card; do not read all four aloud. A middle child solves any card in 2.5 to 4 minutes; the Coins card can take longer, so a pair still stuck keeps its card for round 2. At minute 17 pairs swap with another pair for a 4-minute second round (see the next slide). Reporting back is optional: one thing you tried, not the answer. Answers: Coins) 20¢ + 20¢ + 5¢ (the only way). Patterns) 32: add 3 each time, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26, 29, 32. Logic) Mei, Ben, Sam, Ali. Measuring) 16 cubes: the pen is 10 cubes, and 6 + 10 = 16.

l10-explore2.note: Minutes 17 to 28. 17 to 18: pairs swap cards. 18 to 22: second round (4 minutes). Then ask ONE debrief question: "What helped you when you were stuck?" Take 20-second pair reports from volunteers, one thing they tried, not the answer. Questions 1 and 2 are not asked. Answers: 1) Open answers. 2) Open answers. 3) An inquirer rule: notice, test, check, explain.

l10-teach1.note: Teach: the idea and why. "Today's puzzles mix everything we have learned. Clever inquirers do not know every answer straight away. They know how to START." Click each card and give one example from our lessons: Draw it (the queue in Lesson 5, the bars in Lesson 9). List it (the coin tables in Lesson 6). Make a table (the snail in Lesson 5, patterns in Lesson 1). Click the last box and read it together. The next three slides show each start in action.

l10-we1.note: Worked example: draw it. Ask first: "Can you hold all of this in your head?" Click step 1, then Jo and Ravi appear. Think-aloud: "I draw a line with tall at the top. Jo is taller than Ravi, so Jo is higher. I leave a space in case someone goes between." Step 2, then Lin. Step 3, then Kai: "Shorter than Jo but taller than Ravi: that is the space I left." Answer: read the line from the bottom: Lin. Check each clue against the drawing aloud. The worksheet Q6 uses older and younger: same drawing, oldest at the top.

l10-we2.note: Worked example: list it. Think-aloud: "I could grab coins at random, but then I might miss a way. So I go in order, biggest coin first. 50¢ is already too much. With the 20¢: 20 and 10 is 30, not enough; 20 and both 10s is 40, yes. Now without the 20¢: only the two 10s, that is 20, too little. I have tried everything, so there is only one way." This is the method for worksheet Q4b (a different set of coins), and for counting triangles later.

l10-we3.note: Worked example: make a table. Think-aloud: "I want the 10th number, so I need to know which place each number is in. A table keeps the places tidy. The rule is add 3: I checked every pair, not just the first. 13 is in place 4. Then 16, 19, 22, 25, 28, 31. Place 10 is 31." Count the places aloud with the children so no one skips one. Common mistake: counting the jumps instead of the places (10 numbers have only 9 jumps). Your turn: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20. The 7th number is 20.

l10-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Rushing: not checking the answer against every clue. (2) Q1: finding the rule from the first pair only. (3) Q3c and Q4b: stopping at the first pair or set that works without listing them all. (4) Q5b: counting only the 3 small triangles. (5) Q7: undoing in the wrong order. (6) Q8b: adding 6 + 4 instead of 6 + 10.

l10-break.note: Four minutes. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

l10-teachgraph.note: Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q3 is a picture graph). Click each step after children try it on their own paper (ticked against the answer slide). Step 1: "How many more" means the difference: the 3 apples that stick out past the pears. Step 3: list the pairs in order so none are missed: apples with pears (9), plums (11 ✓), figs (10); then pears with plums (8), figs (7); plums with figs (9). Only apples and plums make 11. Total check: 6 + 3 = 9, 9 + 5 = 14, 14 + 4 = 18.

l10-ws1.note: Minutes 41 to 53. Walk around. Ask "How did you start?" and "How do you know?" before giving any help. Q2 is like the cube method from Lesson 2. Q4b: check pairs list in order. At minute 41 read questions 1 and 2 aloud, then pairs read the rest. The workbook says: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group; invite the WHOLE group at once, for example: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

l10-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains how they started. Q1: 3 → 8 → 13 → 18, add 5 each time: 23, 28. Q2: take away the extra 2: 10 left, share: 5 and 5, give back 2: 5 and 7. Check 5 + 7 = 12. Q3: a) cats 7 − birds 5 = 2. b) 4 + 7 + 3 + 5 = 19. c) list the pairs: only cat and fish make 7 + 3 = 10. Q4: a) 20 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 50. b) with 20¢: 20 + 10 = 30, 20 + 10 + 5 = 35 ✓. Reset (about 30 seconds, taken from this slot): when the answers are checked, everyone stands, reaches up high, shakes out their hands, takes one slow breath and sits down again, then page 2. Skip it if you are more than a minute behind.

l10-teachtri.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5). Click: step 1, then each small triangle lights up as you count. Step 2, then the whole outline. Step 3. Think-aloud: "I count in order: the smallest first, then ones made of two pieces, then three pieces. That way I do not miss the big one or count one twice." The teaching picture has TWO lines from the top (the worksheet picture has one, so it is easier): ask "What are the smallest ones? Which ones are made of two?" Your turn (a shape riddle like Q5a): a rectangle. A square has all 4 sides the same, so it does not fit "only the opposite sides".

l10-teachlen.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q8). Click the ruler bar, step 1, the end-to-end bar, step 2. Think-aloud: "7 longer is not the ruler's length: it is the extra bit. The ruler is the crayon's 5 and 7 more: 12. End to end means both whole lengths: 5 + 12 = 17." Common mistake: 5 + 7 = 12 given as the end-to-end answer.

l10-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up. Q9 (make a puzzle for a friend) is written on this page, about 3 to 4 minutes at the end: check that the puzzle has exactly one answer and that the child can say how to start it. The three re-teach slides (picture graph, triangles, length) are optional reminders: show one only if a child asks.

l10-ws2ans.note: Click each answer after a child explains how they started. Q5b (one line from the top corner, picture on the page): 2 small triangles and 1 big one made of both = 3. The 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 count is the teaching picture with two lines. Q6: line, oldest at the top: Ali, Ben, Mei. Q7: undo the last step first: 10 + 4 = 14, 14 − 9 = 5. Check 5 + 9 = 14, 14 − 4 = 10. Q8: pen 6 + 4 = 10; end to end 6 + 10 = 16. First, everyone stands up and stretches for about a minute (reach up high, touch your toes, shake out your hands) so there is some movement before talk time.

l10-stretch.note: For any pair that chooses to try more (these are on the slide only; Think harder T1 to T4 are in the workbook). Answers: 1) Two ways: five pieces of 2 cubes; or two pieces of 3 cubes and two pieces of 2 cubes (3 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 10). Three pieces of 3 leave 1 over, and one piece of 3 leaves 7, which 2s cannot fill. 2) Ben, Mei, Ali, Sam. 3) Three 10¢ and four 5¢ (30 + 20 = 50).

l10-challenge.note: For any pair that chooses Go further. Use it as a pair choice, or with volunteers in talk time (never call a child by name). Ask for the reason every time. Q3 is open: there is no single right answer, so ask children to check each other's work. Answers: 1) 7, 13, 19, 25 and 31. They go up by 6 (the 2 and the 3 from the two patterns meet every 6). For example 7 sticks make 3 triangles or 2 squares. 2) Ali 8, Ben 12, Mei 9. 3) Open. Check that the new puzzle can be solved and that the child explains the link between the change and the new answer. Example: change "Make 45¢ with exactly 3 coins" (20¢ + 20¢ + 5¢) to "Make 45¢ with exactly 4 coins": now the only way is 20¢ + 10¢ + 10¢ + 5¢.

l10-chdiag.note: Show this picture slide only if a pair asks for it, or is stuck on Go further. The pictures show each problem, not its answer. Ask: What do you notice? What do we know? What do we not know yet? Can you draw or build it? Do not point out the answer; wait for a child to find a pattern.

l10-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Reveal one answer at a time and ask a child to explain before you click. Many children stop at one answer: ask "Is there another way?" and "How do you know you found them all?" For Q3, ask two pairs to swap puzzles and solve each other's.

l10-talk.note: Minutes 71 to 79. Plan: swap puzzles and solve (about 2.5 minutes), 2-minute pair talk, then volunteers. Q9 was written on worksheet page 2. Pairs talk for 2 minutes. Then ask for volunteers first ("Who would like to share?"), never call a child by name to answer, and say that passing is always fine. No tallies and no rankings. Praise the reasons, not only the answers.

l10-exit.note: Minutes 79 to 84. Answer: Open. Use it to plan next steps. Extension: Write a challenge puzzle for next year’s group.

end.note: Minutes 84 to 87. Hand out certificates. Say the certificate line ONCE to the whole group, then spend about 10 seconds on each child with one specific thing they did well. Ask “which puzzle did you enjoy?” as a thumbs-up question, or only of volunteers: do not go round every child. Give parents the one-page summary from the tutor guide. The look-back follows at minute 87 and is never shortened.

l10-reflect.note: Minutes 87 to 90 (3 minutes, after the exit ticket). Children tick or write the Look-back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share their boxes. Praise the strategy ("Drawing it got you unstuck"), not the speed. The "Next time I will try" row is optional and is never marked; at the start of the next lesson the tutor may say, to the whole group, "Today you could try drawing it, using objects or checking your answer" without naming anyone. Say: "Tick what was hard and what helped you. Write or draw one thing you did well. Then tick one thing you might try next time, if you like. You can pass."
